subtopics.title: CloudHub Overview
subtopics.meta_description: Learn what CloudHub is, how its multi-tenant worker architecture works, and how it compares to Runtime Fabric and on-premise Mule deployments.
subtopics.summary: CloudHub is MuleSoft's fully-managed, multi-tenant integration Platform as a Service (iPaaS) for running Mule applications in the cloud.
subtopics.content_html:
CloudHub is MuleSoft's fully-managed integration Platform as a Service (iPaaS). Instead of provisioning and patching your own servers, you deploy Mule applications directly to workers that MuleSoft hosts and operates on AWS infrastructure across a number of global regions. For most organizations that do not have strict data-residency or network-isolation requirements, CloudHub is the fastest way to get an integration into production.

What CloudHub Actually Is

Under the hood, CloudHub runs each deployed application inside one or more isolated workers. A worker is a dedicated Mule runtime instance with its own memory, CPU allocation, and file system, running inside a container that CloudHub manages for you. Because each application gets its own worker(s), a memory leak or crash in one application does not affect any other application running on the platform — this is the "multi-tenant but isolated" model that distinguishes CloudHub from simply running Mule on a shared server.

Worker Sizes and vCores

Workers are sized in vCores, which represent a bundle of CPU and memory. A 0.1 vCore worker is suitable for lightweight development and testing, while production workloads typically run on 0.2 vCore or larger, scaling up as message volume and payload size grow. You can vertically scale a worker (increase its vCore size) or horizontally scale by adding more worker instances behind CloudHub's built-in load balancer.

Key CloudHub Capabilities

  • Elastic scaling — add or remove workers, or resize existing ones, with a redeploy or through the Runtime Manager API.
  • High availability — run multiple workers across different availability zones so that a single infrastructure failure does not take an application down.
  • Built-in load balancing — CloudHub provides a shared load balancer for free, and a dedicated load balancer (with custom domains and TLS) as an add-on.
  • VPC support — deploy workers into a Virtual Private Cloud so they can reach on-premise systems over VPN or Direct Connect, and so on-premise systems cannot be reached from the public internet.
  • Automatic worker monitoring and restart — CloudHub restarts a worker automatically if the Mule runtime inside it becomes unresponsive.
  • Object Store — a managed key-value store used for persistent state (e.g., watermarking in polling flows, idempotent message filtering) that survives worker restarts.

Regions

CloudHub is available in multiple geographic regions (for example US East, US West, EU Ireland, EU Frankfurt, Japan, Australia, and others). Choosing the right region matters for latency to your backend systems and, in many industries, for data-residency and compliance requirements.

CloudHub vs Runtime Fabric vs On-Premise

AspectCloudHubRuntime FabricOn-Premise
Infrastructure managementFully managed by MuleSoftYou manage the underlying VMs/Kubernetes; MuleSoft manages the container platformYou manage everything
Hosting locationMuleSoft-owned AWS environmentYour cloud account or data centerYour data center
ScalingElastic, self-serviceElastic, self-serviceManual
Best forFast time-to-market, standard workloadsData residency + cloud elasticityStrict compliance, legacy infrastructure

Why It Matters

Because CloudHub abstracts away infrastructure concerns, integration developers can focus on flow design, data transformation, and API contracts rather than server patching or capacity planning. It integrates natively with Anypoint Runtime Manager for deployment, monitoring, alerting, and log access, and with Anypoint Exchange and API Manager for the rest of the API lifecycle.

Tip: Even though CloudHub removes infrastructure management, you are still responsible for sizing workers correctly and monitoring memory/CPU usage — an under-sized worker is one of the most common causes of production incidents.

Key Points

  • CloudHub is MuleSoft's managed, multi-tenant iPaaS built on AWS.
  • Each deployed application runs in one or more isolated workers sized in vCores.
  • CloudHub offers elastic scaling, high availability, VPC networking, and managed Object Stores out of the box.
  • Region selection affects latency and compliance.
  • CloudHub differs from Runtime Fabric mainly in who owns and manages the underlying infrastructure.

subtopics.title: CloudHub 1.0 Architecture
subtopics.meta_description: How CloudHub 1.0's worker-based deployment model works on AWS, including vCore sizing, shared and dedicated load balancing, static IPs, and its limitations.
subtopics.summary: CloudHub 1.0 deploys each Mule application to one or more dedicated worker virtual machines running on AWS infrastructure managed entirely by MuleSoft.
subtopics.content_html:
CloudHub 1.0 was, for years, the default way organizations ran Mule applications without managing any infrastructure themselves. Understanding its worker-based model still matters, both because many organizations continue to run it in production and because it clarifies exactly what CloudHub 2.0 changed later.

The Worker Model

In CloudHub 1.0, every deployed application runs on one or more workers — dedicated virtual machines provisioned on AWS EC2 infrastructure that MuleSoft owns and manages. Critically, workers are allocated per application: one worker runs exactly one application, and that application does not share its VM with any other tenant's application. This gives strong isolation between applications, at the cost of granularity — you can't run five lightweight applications on fractions of a single shared machine.

Each worker runs a full Mule runtime instance. When an application is configured to run with multiple workers, CloudHub automatically load-balances traffic across them and can restart an unhealthy worker without operator intervention, giving basic high-availability out of the box once more than one worker is provisioned.

vCore Sizing

Workers are sized in vCores, a CloudHub-specific unit of compute and memory capacity rather than a literal CPU core count. Available sizes typically range from 0.1 vCores (suitable for lightweight, low-traffic applications) up to 8 vCores or more for demanding workloads. Choosing a worker size is a tradeoff between cost and headroom: undersized workers show up as memory pressure or slow garbage collection under load, while oversized workers waste allocated capacity that is billed regardless of whether it's used.

Load Balancing and Static IPs

By default, applications deployed to CloudHub 1.0 get a shared load balancer, sitting in front of multiple customers' applications and providing basic HTTPS termination and routing, at no additional cost. For applications with specific requirements — a custom TLS certificate, dedicated static IP addresses for partner allowlisting, or finer control over load balancing behavior — organizations can provision a dedicated load balancer instead, at additional cost.

Static IP addresses matter in practice because many partner integrations require IP allowlisting on their end before they'll accept traffic; CloudHub 1.0 supports reserving static IPs for outbound and inbound traffic specifically to satisfy that requirement.

Deployment Model

Deploying to CloudHub 1.0 typically means pushing a compiled Mule application deployable archive (a JAR file produced by the Mule Maven Plugin) to the platform, either via the Runtime Manager console, Anypoint CLI, or the Maven plugin's deploy goal. CloudHub then provisions the configured number of workers at the configured vCore size, deploys the application to each, and brings it online behind the load balancer.

anypoint-cli-v4 runtime-mgr:application:deploy orders-api \
  target/orders-api-1.0.0-mule-application.jar \
  --runtime 4.4.0 \
  --workers 2 \
  --workerSize 0.2 \
  --environment Production

Limitations

The one-application-per-worker model has real drawbacks. Deploying a new version typically takes several minutes because a full new worker VM needs to spin up before traffic shifts over, and running many small applications means paying for many separate VMs even when their combined actual load is modest. vCore allocation is also fairly coarse-grained compared to container-based scaling, and workers are tied to specific AWS regions, meaning multi-region deployment requires separate application deployments per region rather than one deployment spanning several.

  • CloudHub 1.0 runs each application on one or more dedicated worker VMs on AWS, with strict per-application isolation.
  • Worker capacity is sized in vCores, a CloudHub-specific compute/memory unit rather than literal CPU cores.
  • A free shared load balancer is provided by default; dedicated load balancers add custom TLS and static IP support.
  • Multiple workers provide basic high availability and automatic load balancing without extra configuration.
  • Deployment is comparatively slow since a full worker VM must boot before a new version goes live, and scaling is coarse-grained.

subtopics.title: CloudHub 2.0 Architecture
subtopics.meta_description: How CloudHub 2.0's containerized, Kubernetes-based architecture replaces dedicated workers with replicas for faster, more granular deployments overall.
subtopics.summary: CloudHub 2.0 replaces CloudHub 1.0's dedicated worker VMs with containerized replicas running on a Kubernetes-based platform for faster, more granular deployments.
subtopics.content_html:
CloudHub 2.0 rebuilds the same basic promise as CloudHub 1.0 — fully managed deployment with no infrastructure to maintain — on a fundamentally different foundation: containers orchestrated by Kubernetes instead of dedicated virtual machines.

Replicas Instead of Workers

Where CloudHub 1.0 provisions dedicated VM-based workers, CloudHub 2.0 deploys applications as containerized replicas running as pods on a shared, MuleSoft-managed Kubernetes cluster. Each replica still runs one Mule application, preserving the same application-level isolation model conceptually, but the underlying compute is a container rather than a full VM — which is what unlocks faster startup and more efficient resource use, since containers start in seconds rather than the minutes a fresh VM boot requires.

What Changed, Side by Side

AspectCloudHub 1.0CloudHub 2.0
Compute unitDedicated worker VM (AWS EC2)Containerized replica (Kubernetes pod)
Deployment speedSeveral minutes (full VM boot)Seconds to low minutes (container start)
Sizing granularityFixed vCore tiers (0.1, 0.2, 1, 2, 4, 8...)More granular vCPU/memory combinations
Isolation modelOne application per VM, strong hardware-level isolationOne application per replica, container-level isolation
NetworkingShared or dedicated load balancer add-onPrivate Spaces with built-in VPC-style network isolation
Underlying infrastructureAWS EC2 instances managed by MuleSoftKubernetes-based platform managed by MuleSoft
ScalingManual addition of workersReplica count adjustable with finer increments, supports more dynamic scaling

Faster, More Granular Deployments

Because replicas are containers rather than full VMs, redeploying a new application version is noticeably faster — the platform can start new replica containers, confirm they're healthy, and shift traffic over in a fraction of the time a new worker VM would take to boot. This shortens the feedback loop for teams deploying frequently, and it also makes it more practical to right-size applications, since vCPU and memory can be allocated more granularly than CloudHub 1.0's fixed vCore tiers allowed.

Improved Isolation with Private Spaces

CloudHub 2.0 introduces Private Spaces, a network isolation boundary conceptually similar to a VPC, within which an organization's applications run isolated from other customers' workloads at the network layer, not just the application layer. This makes it straightforward to set up private connectivity to on-premises systems or other cloud VPCs (via VPN or peering) without the address space and routing constraints that existed in CloudHub 1.0's shared network model.

Deployment Example

anypoint-cli-v4 runtime-mgr:application:deploy orders-api \
  target/orders-api-1.0.0-mule-application.jar \
  --target cloudhub2-space-us-east-1 \
  --runtime 4.6.0 \
  --replicas 2 \
  --vCores 0.2 \
  --environment Production

Migration Considerations

CloudHub 2.0 is not simply a drop-in replacement for CloudHub 1.0 applications; migrating typically requires reviewing static IP dependencies (since IP allocation works differently under Private Spaces), re-provisioning environment configuration under the new target, and validating that any CloudHub 1.0-specific features an application relies on have an equivalent in CloudHub 2.0. Most organizations run a migration project rather than a simple redeploy-and-switch.

  • CloudHub 2.0 replaces dedicated VM workers with containerized replicas running on a Kubernetes-based platform.
  • Container-based replicas start dramatically faster than CloudHub 1.0 worker VMs, shortening deployment time.
  • Sizing is more granular, allowing finer vCPU/memory allocation than CloudHub 1.0's fixed vCore tiers.
  • Private Spaces add network-layer isolation and simplify private connectivity to on-prem or other cloud networks.
  • Moving an application from CloudHub 1.0 to 2.0 is a migration project, not an automatic drop-in switch.

subtopics.title: Deploying to CloudHub
subtopics.meta_description: A step-by-step guide to deploying Mule applications to CloudHub using Anypoint Studio, Anypoint CLI, Maven, and Runtime Manager.
subtopics.summary: There are several supported ways to deploy a Mule application to CloudHub, from Anypoint Studio's right-click deploy to Maven and Anypoint CLI for automated pipelines.
subtopics.content_html:
Once you have a Mule application ready, MuleSoft gives you several ways to get it running on CloudHub. Which method you choose usually depends on where you are in the development lifecycle: interactive deployment from Anypoint Studio while developing, and scripted deployment via Maven or Anypoint CLI once you move toward CI/CD.

Method 1: Deploy from Anypoint Studio

The simplest way to deploy is directly from Anypoint Studio. Right-click the project in Package Explorer, choose Anypoint Platform > Deploy to CloudHub, and fill in the deployment form: application name (must be globally unique — it becomes part of the CloudHub domain), environment, region, runtime version, and worker size/count. Studio packages the application, uploads it, and Runtime Manager takes care of provisioning workers and starting the application.

Method 2: Deploy with the Mule Maven Plugin

For repeatable, scriptable deployments, most teams configure the mule-maven-plugin in the project's pom.xml and run a Maven goal. This is the approach almost universally used inside CI/CD pipelines.

<plugin>
  <groupId>org.mule.tools.maven</groupId>
  <artifactId>mule-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>4.1.0</version>
  <extensions>true</extensions>
  <configuration>
    <cloudHubDeployment>
      <uri>https://anypoint.mulesoft.com</uri>
      <muleVersion>4.4.0</muleVersion>
      <username>${env.ANYPOINT_USER}</username>
      <password>${env.ANYPOINT_PASS}</password>
      <applicationName>order-api-dev</applicationName>
      <environment>Development</environment>
      <region>us-east-1</region>
      <workerType>MICRO</workerType>
      <workers>1</workers>
    </cloudHubDeployment>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

With that plugin configured, deployment is a single command:

mvn clean deploy -DmuleDeploy

Method 3: Deploy with Anypoint CLI

Anypoint CLI (anypoint-cli) is a Node.js-based command line tool that wraps the Platform APIs and is handy for ad-hoc deployments or scripting outside of Maven.

anypoint-cli-v4 runtime-mgr:application:deploy   order-api-dev   ./target/order-api-1.0.0-mule-application.jar   --runtime 4.4.0   --workerSize 0.1   --workers 1   --environment Development   --region us-east-1

Method 4: Deploy from Runtime Manager UI

You can also upload a packaged .jar file directly through the Runtime Manager console — useful when someone outside the development team needs to promote a build without touching a terminal.

What Happens During Deployment

  1. The application is packaged into a deployable archive (a Mule application .jar) by the Mule Maven Plugin.
  2. The archive is uploaded to CloudHub.
  3. CloudHub provisions the requested number of workers of the requested size.
  4. The Mule runtime starts inside each worker and deploys the application.
  5. Health checks confirm the application started successfully; if not, the deployment is marked failed and the previous version (if any) may remain running depending on configuration.

Naming, Environments, and Domains

Every CloudHub application name must be globally unique across all CloudHub tenants because it forms part of the default DNS entry: <app-name>.<region>.cloudhub.io. A common convention is to suffix the application name with the environment, e.g. order-api-dev, order-api-qa, order-api-prod, which also keeps deployments to different Anypoint Platform environments clearly separated.

Note: Deploying the same application name to the same environment again performs a redeploy (zero or near-zero downtime depending on configuration), not a fresh provisioning.

Key Points

  • You can deploy to CloudHub from Anypoint Studio, Maven (mule-maven-plugin), Anypoint CLI, or the Runtime Manager UI.
  • Maven-based deployment is the standard approach for CI/CD automation.
  • Application names must be globally unique and typically encode the environment.
  • Runtime Manager provisions workers, starts the Mule runtime, and performs health checks after every deployment.

subtopics.title: Runtime Fabric
subtopics.meta_description: Understand Anypoint Runtime Fabric: MuleSoft's container-based deployment option that runs on your own cloud infrastructure or on-premise.
subtopics.summary: Runtime Fabric is a container orchestration layer, built on Kubernetes, that lets you run Mule applications on infrastructure you own while MuleSoft manages the runtime platform.
subtopics.content_html:
Anypoint Runtime Fabric (RTF) sits between CloudHub and a fully self-managed on-premise deployment. It gives you CloudHub-like self-service deployment and elastic scaling, but the underlying compute runs on infrastructure that you control — your own AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud account, or your own data center.

What Runtime Fabric Is

Runtime Fabric is a container orchestration platform built on Kubernetes. MuleSoft provides the installer and ongoing lifecycle management for the Runtime Fabric agents, but you provision and own the virtual machines (or bare-metal hosts) that Runtime Fabric runs on. Applications are deployed as Docker-style containers, each replica running inside its own isolated container, scheduled across the Runtime Fabric cluster by Kubernetes underneath.

Why Organizations Choose Runtime Fabric

  • Data residency — keep application processing and any data-in-motion inside your own cloud region or country, satisfying regulatory requirements CloudHub's fixed regions might not meet.
  • Network access to internal systems — when applications need direct, low-latency access to on-premise or private-cloud systems without VPN/VPC tunnels.
  • Consistent platform experience — teams still get self-service deployment, autoscaling, and centralized monitoring through Anypoint Runtime Manager, the same console used for CloudHub.
  • Cost control at scale — for very large deployments, running on your own reserved cloud capacity can be more cost-effective than CloudHub's worker-based pricing.

Where Runtime Fabric Runs

Runtime Fabric can be installed on:

  • Customer-managed VMs in AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud Platform.
  • Existing customer-managed Kubernetes clusters (Runtime Fabric on Kubernetes).
  • On-premise VMware or bare-metal infrastructure, for organizations that need integration workloads to stay entirely inside their own data center while still getting a modern deployment experience.

Deploying an Application to Runtime Fabric

From a developer's perspective, deploying to Runtime Fabric looks nearly identical to deploying to CloudHub — you target a Runtime Fabric deployment target instead of CloudHub workers, either through Runtime Manager, Anypoint CLI, or the Mule Maven Plugin.

anypoint-cli-v4 runtime-mgr:application:deploy   order-api-prod   ./target/order-api-1.0.0-mule-application.jar   --target my-rtf-cluster   --replicas 2   --cpuReserved 500m   --memoryReserved 1000Mi   --environment Production

Key concepts unique to Runtime Fabric deployments include replicas (equivalent to CloudHub workers — how many container instances run the application) and CPU/memory reservations and limits, expressed in Kubernetes-style units.

Runtime Fabric vs CloudHub

AspectCloudHubRuntime Fabric
Infrastructure ownerMuleSoftYou (your cloud account or data center)
Underlying techProprietary CloudHub workersKubernetes-based containers
Data residency controlLimited to available CloudHub regionsAny region/data center you can host in
Operational overheadNone — fully managedYou patch/maintain the host VMs; MuleSoft manages the RTF software
Management consoleAnypoint Runtime ManagerAnypoint Runtime Manager (same console)

High Availability and Scaling

Because Runtime Fabric is Kubernetes-based, it inherits Kubernetes' self-healing behavior: if a container crashes, Kubernetes restarts it automatically; if a host node fails, workloads are rescheduled onto healthy nodes (as capacity allows). You configure the number of replicas per application and, at the cluster level, how many nodes make up the Runtime Fabric cluster.

Tip: Runtime Fabric requires you to manage patching and capacity of the underlying VMs yourself — it is not a zero-infrastructure option like CloudHub, even though the deployment experience feels similar.

Key Points

  • Runtime Fabric is a Kubernetes-based container platform you host, with the platform layer managed by MuleSoft.
  • It is chosen mainly for data residency, network proximity to internal systems, and large-scale cost control.
  • Deployment and monitoring go through the same Anypoint Runtime Manager console used for CloudHub.
  • Scaling is expressed as container replicas plus CPU/memory reservations, rather than CloudHub's vCore worker sizes.

subtopics.title: Standalone and Hybrid Deployment
subtopics.meta_description: How standalone Mule runtime deployment on-premises works, what hybrid deployment mixes in from CloudHub, and why organizations choose this deployment model.
subtopics.summary: Standalone Mule runtimes run entirely under an organization's own infrastructure, and hybrid deployment pairs that self-hosted runtime with CloudHub's cloud-based control plane.
subtopics.content_html:
Not every organization can or wants to run its integration workloads in MuleSoft's cloud. Regulatory requirements, data residency rules, existing data center investment, or simply the need to run integrations physically close to on-premises systems all push toward running the Mule runtime itself outside of CloudHub — which is exactly what standalone and hybrid deployment support.

Standalone Deployment

A standalone deployment runs the Mule runtime directly on infrastructure the organization controls — a physical server, an on-prem virtual machine, or a VM in a private or public cloud account that isn't CloudHub. The runtime is downloaded and installed like any other server software, applications are deployed to it directly (via the command line, a deployment script, or CI/CD tooling), and the organization is fully responsible for provisioning, patching, scaling, and monitoring that infrastructure. There is no CloudHub involvement in a purely standalone setup at all — not even for management.

# installing and starting a standalone Mule runtime
tar -xzf mule-ee-distribution-4.6.0.tar.gz
cd mule-enterprise-standalone-4.6.0
./bin/mule start

# deploying an application to the standalone runtime
cp target/orders-api-1.0.0-mule-application.jar apps/

This model gives an organization complete control over the runtime's environment, network placement, and patch schedule, at the cost of taking on all of the operational burden that CloudHub would otherwise absorb.

Hybrid Deployment

A hybrid deployment is a middle ground: the Mule runtime itself still runs on self-hosted infrastructure (the same as a standalone deployment), but the runtime registers with Anypoint Platform's Runtime Manager, giving the organization a single management, monitoring, and deployment console across both its self-hosted runtimes and any CloudHub-hosted applications it also runs. In effect, the control plane lives in the cloud (Anypoint Platform) while the data plane — where the actual Mule application executes and processes messages — stays on-premises or in a private cloud account the organization controls.

This is achieved by installing a Mule runtime and registering it as a server (or grouping several as a server group or cluster) within Runtime Manager, after which applications can be deployed to it from Anypoint Platform exactly as they would be deployed to CloudHub, even though the actual compute never leaves the organization's own network.

Why Organizations Choose This Over Full CloudHub

  • Data residency and regulatory constraints — some industries or jurisdictions require certain data to never leave specific physical infrastructure or geographic boundaries that CloudHub's available regions don't satisfy.
  • Proximity to on-premises systems — integrations that talk heavily to mainframes, on-prem databases, or legacy systems benefit from running on the same network, avoiding the latency and firewall complexity of reaching back from the cloud on every call.
  • Existing infrastructure investment — organizations with substantial data center capacity already in place, or with cloud commitments to a provider other than AWS (which underlies CloudHub 1.0), often prefer to run Mule alongside their other workloads rather than adopt an additional cloud footprint.
  • Air-gapped or highly restricted networks — environments with no permitted outbound internet connectivity at all sometimes require standalone deployment without even the hybrid model's Runtime Manager registration.

Trade-offs to Weigh

The operational cost of standalone and hybrid deployment is real: patching the runtime, scaling capacity, handling failover, and securing the host all become the organization's responsibility rather than MuleSoft's. Hybrid deployment reduces some of this burden by centralizing visibility and deployment orchestration in Anypoint Platform, but the underlying servers, their OS, and their availability still need to be managed directly. Many organizations that start standalone eventually move toward Runtime Fabric (a self-hosted, Kubernetes-based alternative to CloudHub 2.0) specifically to regain some of the automated scaling and deployment speed that pure standalone deployment lacks, while still keeping compute on their own infrastructure.

  • Standalone deployment runs the Mule runtime entirely on self-managed infrastructure, with no CloudHub involvement.
  • Hybrid deployment keeps the runtime self-hosted but registers it with Anypoint Platform's Runtime Manager for centralized management.
  • Hybrid separates the control plane (cloud-based Anypoint Platform) from the data plane (on-premises runtime execution).
  • Data residency, proximity to legacy systems, and existing infrastructure investment are the most common reasons to choose this model.
  • Both models shift operational responsibility (patching, scaling, failover) from MuleSoft to the organization running the servers.

subtopics.title: On-Premise Deployment
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how to install and run the Mule standalone runtime on your own servers, including clustering and hybrid connectivity to Anypoint Platform.
subtopics.summary: On-premise deployment runs the Mule standalone runtime directly on servers you own, giving full infrastructure control at the cost of manual scaling and patching.
subtopics.content_html:
Before CloudHub and Runtime Fabric existed, running Mule applications meant installing the Mule runtime on your own Linux or Windows servers — and that option, often called a standalone or on-premise deployment, is still widely used today, particularly by organizations with strict data-sovereignty rules, air-gapped networks, or existing data-center investments they need to keep using.

What On-Premise Deployment Means

You download the Mule Enterprise Edition runtime distribution, install it on a server you control, and deploy application archives to it directly — either by dropping a packaged .jar into the runtime's apps directory or by using Anypoint CLI/Maven configured to target that standalone server. Everything from OS patching, JVM tuning, disk space, and network configuration to backup and disaster recovery is your responsibility.

Installing the Standalone Runtime

# Extract the downloaded runtime distribution
unzip mule-ee-distribution-standalone-4.4.0.zip -d /opt/mule

# Start the runtime
cd /opt/mule/mule-enterprise-standalone-4.4.0/bin
./mule start

# Deploy an application by copying the packaged jar
cp order-api-1.0.0-mule-application.jar /opt/mule/mule-enterprise-standalone-4.4.0/apps/

The runtime automatically detects new or updated .jar files in the apps directory and hot-deploys them without a full server restart.

Connecting to Anypoint Platform (Hybrid Model)

An on-premise Mule runtime can still register with Anypoint Platform as a server (or a member of a server group/cluster) so that it appears in Runtime Manager for centralized monitoring, alerting, and log access — even though MuleSoft never touches the underlying machine. This is commonly called a hybrid deployment: application runtime on-premise, management plane in the cloud.

./amc_setup.sh -H proxyHost -P proxyPort   -cn Production   <registration-token>

Clustering for High Availability

Because there is no built-in elastic scaling like CloudHub or Runtime Fabric, high availability on-premise is achieved by configuring a Mule cluster: multiple standalone runtime nodes that share state (such as VM queues or polling watermarks) and can fail over to one another. Clustering is configured through Runtime Manager or the mule command with cluster-specific flags, and typically sits behind an external load balancer that you also own and configure (e.g., NGINX, F5, or a hardware load balancer).

Trade-offs vs Managed Options

FactorOn-PremiseCloudHub / Runtime Fabric
Infrastructure controlFullPartial (RTF) / None (CloudHub)
ScalingManual (add nodes, resize VMs)Self-service / elastic
Patching & upgradesYour responsibilityRuntime patching largely automated
Load balancingYou provide and configureBuilt in
Best fitLegacy data centers, strict isolationFaster delivery, less operational burden

When On-Premise Still Makes Sense

  • Regulatory or contractual requirements that prohibit any cloud-hosted processing of certain data.
  • Legacy mainframe or AS/400 integrations that require the Mule runtime to sit physically close to the source system.
  • Organizations mid-way through a cloud migration that still need to support existing data-center investments.
Note: Even fully on-premise deployments typically still connect back to Anypoint Platform for centralized API Manager governance and Exchange cataloging — it is rare to run Mule completely disconnected from the control plane.

Key Points

  • On-premise deployment installs the standalone Mule runtime on servers you fully own and manage.
  • Applications are deployed by placing packaged jars in the runtime's apps directory, or via CLI/Maven.
  • A hybrid model lets on-premise servers register with Anypoint Runtime Manager for monitoring without moving compute to the cloud.
  • High availability requires manually configured clustering and an externally provided load balancer.

subtopics.title: Deploying via Anypoint CLI
subtopics.meta_description: How to install and authenticate anypoint-cli-v4, then deploy a Mule application from the command line using runtime-mgr:application:deploy and scripts.
subtopics.summary: Anypoint CLI lets teams deploy and manage Mule applications from a terminal or script, making it a natural fit for automation outside a full CI/CD pipeline.
subtopics.content_html:
Not every deployment needs a full pipeline behind it. For quick deployments, local scripting, or lightweight automation, Anypoint CLI gives direct command-line access to the same deployment and management operations available through Runtime Manager's UI.

Installing anypoint-cli-v4

The CLI is distributed as an npm package and requires Node.js to be installed first.

npm install -g anypoint-cli-v4

# verify installation
anypoint-cli-v4 --version

Authenticating

The CLI supports interactive login as well as non-interactive authentication suited to scripts, using either a Connected App (client credentials) or a username/password combination. For automation, a Connected App with the minimum required scopes is the safer option, since it can be revoked independently of any individual user's account.

# interactive login (prompts for credentials)
anypoint-cli-v4 account:login

# non-interactive, using a Connected App's client credentials
anypoint-cli-v4 account:login \
  --client_id "$ANYPOINT_CLIENT_ID" \
  --client_secret "$ANYPOINT_CLIENT_SECRET"

Credentials should always come from environment variables or a secrets manager in scripted contexts — never hardcoded directly into a deployment script that might end up in version control.

Deploying an Application

The core deployment command is runtime-mgr:application:deploy, which takes the application name, the path to the deployable JAR built by the Mule Maven Plugin, and a set of flags describing the target runtime, sizing, and environment.

anypoint-cli-v4 runtime-mgr:application:deploy orders-api \
  target/orders-api-1.0.0-mule-application.jar \
  --runtime 4.6.0 \
  --workers 2 \
  --workerSize 0.2 \
  --environment Production \
  --businessGroup "Integration Team" \
  --property "db.host=orders-db.internal.example.com" \
  --property "log.level=INFO"

Key flags worth understanding: --runtime pins the exact Mule runtime version rather than letting it default, which matters for reproducibility; --workers and --workerSize control worker count and vCore sizing on CloudHub 1.0 (CloudHub 2.0 deployments instead use --target, --replicas, and --vCores); and repeated --property flags inject runtime properties without baking environment-specific values into the packaged JAR.

Checking Deployment Status

After deploying, the CLI can also be used to confirm the application actually came up healthy rather than assuming success just because the deploy command returned.

anypoint-cli-v4 runtime-mgr:application:describe orders-api \
  --environment Production

The output includes the application's current status (STARTED, DEPLOYING, FAILED), assigned worker or replica count, and the runtime version actually running — useful for scripting a wait-and-check loop that confirms the application is healthy before a pipeline reports success, rather than exiting as soon as the deploy call itself returns.

Managing Applications, Not Just Deploying Them

Anypoint CLI covers the rest of an application's lifecycle too, which matters for day-to-day operations beyond the initial deployment: restarting a stuck application, tailing logs during an incident, or removing an application that's no longer needed.

# restart without redeploying
anypoint-cli-v4 runtime-mgr:application:modify orders-api --environment Production --restart

# stream recent logs
anypoint-cli-v4 runtime-mgr:application:log-list orders-api --environment Production

# remove an application entirely
anypoint-cli-v4 runtime-mgr:application:delete orders-api --environment Production

Having these available as ordinary commands means an incident-response runbook can reference exact, copy-pasteable commands instead of a set of UI screenshots that go stale the moment Runtime Manager's interface changes.

Using It in Scripts

Because every operation is a single command with a predictable exit code, Anypoint CLI fits naturally into shell scripts for teams that want scripted, repeatable deployments without adopting a full CI/CD platform, or as a lightweight step inside one. A typical pattern builds the application with Maven first, then deploys the resulting artifact with the CLI, checking the exit status before proceeding.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

mvn clean package -DskipMunitTests=false

anypoint-cli-v4 runtime-mgr:application:deploy orders-api \
  target/orders-api-1.0.0-mule-application.jar \
  --runtime 4.6.0 \
  --workers 2 \
  --workerSize 0.2 \
  --environment Production

echo "Deployment submitted successfully."
  • anypoint-cli-v4 is installed via npm and requires Node.js as a prerequisite.
  • Non-interactive authentication should use a scoped Connected App's client credentials, sourced from environment variables.
  • runtime-mgr:application:deploy takes an application name, a deployable JAR, and flags for runtime version, sizing, and environment.
  • Repeated --property flags inject environment-specific configuration without baking values into the packaged artifact.
  • The CLI's predictable, scriptable command structure makes it well suited to shell-based automation and lightweight pipelines.

subtopics.title: Deploying via the Mule Maven Plugin
subtopics.meta_description: How to configure the mule-maven-plugin in pom.xml for CloudHub, CloudHub 2.0, and Runtime Fabric deployment targets, plus secure credential storage tips.
subtopics.summary: The Mule Maven Plugin lets a single mvn deploy command build and deploy a Mule application to CloudHub, CloudHub 2.0, or Runtime Fabric directly from pom.xml configuration.
subtopics.content_html:
For teams that already build their Mule applications with Maven — which is effectively every Mule 4 project — the Mule Maven Plugin's deployment goals mean the same tool that compiles and packages the application can also deploy it, with the target platform and credentials defined declaratively in pom.xml rather than as separate scripted steps.

Configuring the Plugin for CloudHub

<plugin>
  <groupId>org.mule.tools.maven</groupId>
  <artifactId>mule-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>4.1.0</version>
  <extensions>true</extensions>
  <configuration>
    <cloudHubDeployment>
      <uri>https://anypoint.mulesoft.com</uri>
      <muleVersion>4.6.0</muleVersion>
      <username>${env.ANYPOINT_USERNAME}</username>
      <password>${env.ANYPOINT_PASSWORD}</password>
      <applicationName>orders-api</applicationName>
      <environment>Production</environment>
      <workers>2</workers>
      <workerType>MICRO</workerType>
    </cloudHubDeployment>
  </configuration>
</plugin>

The workerType element (or its numeric vCore equivalent depending on plugin version) controls sizing, while workers controls the count — both map directly to the same values you would otherwise set through Runtime Manager's UI. Keeping them in pom.xml means an infrastructure change like adding a second worker is reviewed and versioned through the same pull-request process as any code change.

Configuring for CloudHub 2.0

CloudHub 2.0 deployments use a distinct configuration block reflecting the replica-based model rather than workers, and typically authenticate via a Connected App instead of a username/password pair.

<configuration>
  <cloudhub2Deployment>
    <uri>https://anypoint.mulesoft.com</uri>
    <muleVersion>4.6.0</muleVersion>
    <provider>MC</provider>
    <target>cloudhub2-space-us-east-1</target>
    <applicationName>orders-api</applicationName>
    <environment>Production</environment>
    <connectedAppClientId>${env.ANYPOINT_CLIENT_ID}</connectedAppClientId>
    <connectedAppClientSecret>${env.ANYPOINT_CLIENT_SECRET}</connectedAppClientSecret>
    <replicas>2</replicas>
    <vCores>0.2</vCores>
  </cloudhub2Deployment>
</configuration>

Configuring for Runtime Fabric

Runtime Fabric deployments (self-hosted container orchestration for on-prem or private cloud) use yet another block, pointing at the target Runtime Fabric instance rather than a CloudHub region.

<configuration>
  <runtimeFabricDeployment>
    <uri>https://anypoint.mulesoft.com</uri>
    <muleVersion>4.6.0</muleVersion>
    <target>my-runtime-fabric</target>
    <applicationName>orders-api</applicationName>
    <environment>Production</environment>
    <connectedAppClientId>${env.ANYPOINT_CLIENT_ID}</connectedAppClientId>
    <connectedAppClientSecret>${env.ANYPOINT_CLIENT_SECRET}</connectedAppClientSecret>
    <replicas>2</replicas>
  </runtimeFabricDeployment>
</configuration>

Deploying

With the plugin configured, deployment is a single Maven command bound to the deploy phase, which first runs the full build (including MUnit tests, if configured) and then deploys the resulting artifact.

mvn clean deploy -DmuleDeploy

Selecting a Target Per Environment with Profiles

Most real projects need to deploy the same artifact to more than one environment — Sandbox, UAT, Production — often with different worker counts, replica counts, or even different deployment targets entirely. Rather than maintaining separate copies of pom.xml, Maven profiles let each environment's deployment block live side by side, activated selectively at build time.

mvn clean deploy -DmuleDeploy -Pproduction-deploy \
  -Denv.ANYPOINT_CLIENT_ID="$PROD_CLIENT_ID" \
  -Denv.ANYPOINT_CLIENT_SECRET="$PROD_CLIENT_SECRET"

Each profile wraps its own cloudHubDeployment, cloudhub2Deployment, or runtimeFabricDeployment block with environment-specific values for applicationName, environment, and sizing, while the surrounding build (compilation, packaging, MUnit execution) stays identical across all of them. This keeps environment differences explicit and reviewable in source control instead of scattered across separate deployment scripts.

Storing Credentials Securely

Hardcoding usernames, passwords, or client secrets directly in pom.xml is a common but avoidable mistake, since pom.xml is committed to version control. Two safer patterns are standard practice: referencing environment variables (as shown above with ${env.ANYPOINT_CLIENT_ID}), which keeps secrets out of the repository entirely and lets a CI/CD platform inject them at build time; or storing encrypted values in Maven's settings.xml using Maven's built-in password encryption, referenced via ${settings.property} style placeholders and decrypted automatically at build time using a locally stored master password.

# create an encrypted master password once
mvn --encrypt-master-password

# encrypt an individual credential for settings.xml
mvn --encrypt-password

Whichever approach is used, the guiding rule is the same: nothing that grants deployment access should ever appear in plaintext inside a file that gets committed to source control.

  • The mule-maven-plugin supports distinct configuration blocks for CloudHub, CloudHub 2.0, and Runtime Fabric deployment targets.
  • CloudHub 2.0 and Runtime Fabric deployments typically authenticate via Connected App client credentials rather than username/password.
  • A single mvn clean deploy -DmuleDeploy command builds and deploys the application once the plugin is configured.
  • Credentials belong in environment variables or encrypted Maven settings.xml entries, never hardcoded in pom.xml.
  • Maven's built-in password encryption (encrypt-master-password / encrypt-password) protects settings.xml credentials at rest.

subtopics.title: CI/CD for Mule Applications
subtopics.meta_description: Design a CI/CD pipeline for Mule 4 applications using Maven, MUnit, and tools like Jenkins, GitHub Actions, or Azure DevOps to deploy across environments.
subtopics.summary: A solid CI/CD pipeline for Mule applications builds with Maven, runs MUnit tests, and promotes the same versioned artifact through Dev, QA, and Production.
subtopics.content_html:
Manually deploying Mule applications from Anypoint Studio works fine for a proof of concept, but production-grade integration teams automate the build, test, and deployment process so that every change is validated consistently and every environment runs a known, versioned artifact. This is where CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery) comes in.

The Core Building Blocks

  • Source control — Mule projects live in Git (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure Repos).
  • Maven — the Mule Maven Plugin builds, packages, tests, and deploys the application; almost every CI/CD pipeline for Mule wraps Maven commands.
  • MUnit — automated tests that run as part of the Maven build (mvn test or the munit:test goal) and fail the pipeline if coverage or assertions fail.
  • A CI/CD orchestrator — Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps, Bamboo, or similar, to trigger builds on commit and coordinate deployment stages.
  • Anypoint Exchange — often used as an artifact repository for reusable connectors and API specifications consumed by multiple pipelines.

A Typical Pipeline Flow

  1. Developer pushes code to a feature branch and opens a pull request.
  2. CI server triggers a build: mvn clean package, running MUnit tests and static analysis.
  3. On merge to the main branch, the pipeline builds again, this time producing a versioned, immutable artifact (the Mule application jar).
  4. The artifact is deployed automatically to a Development or QA environment.
  5. Automated smoke tests or manual QA sign-off gate promotion to UAT/Staging.
  6. A final approval step (often manual) promotes the exact same artifact to Production — never a rebuild.
Tip: Build the artifact once and promote that same binary through every environment. Rebuilding per environment risks subtle differences between what was tested and what ships to production.

Example: GitHub Actions Workflow

name: mule-ci-cd
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build-test-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '8'
      - name: Build and run MUnit tests
        run: mvn clean package
      - name: Deploy to CloudHub Dev
        run: mvn deploy -DmuleDeploy -Denv=dev
        env:
          ANYPOINT_USER: ${{ secrets.ANYPOINT_USER }}
          ANYPOINT_PASS: ${{ secrets.ANYPOINT_PASS }}

Externalizing Environment Configuration

Pipelines should never hard-code environment-specific values (database URLs, client secrets, worker sizes) inside the project. Instead, use Maven profiles or environment variables combined with property placeholders in your Mule configuration, and inject the actual values at deploy time, often from a secrets manager or your CI/CD tool's encrypted variables.

Common Pipeline Stages for Mule Projects

StagePurpose
BuildCompile, resolve dependencies, package as a deployable jar
Unit testRun MUnit suites and enforce minimum coverage
Static analysisLint DataWeave/XML, scan for hard-coded secrets
Deploy to Dev/QAAutomatic on every merge to main
Integration/regression testsRun against the deployed Dev/QA instance
Deploy to ProductionManual approval gate, same artifact promoted

Key Points

  • CI/CD for Mule applications is built around Maven, the Mule Maven Plugin, and MUnit.
  • Build the artifact once and promote the identical binary through Dev, QA, and Production.
  • Externalize environment-specific configuration instead of hard-coding it into the project.
  • Any major CI orchestrator (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, GitLab CI) can drive the pipeline since the underlying commands are just Maven/CLI calls.

subtopics.title: Application Properties and Environments
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how to externalize configuration with property placeholders, YAML/properties files, secure properties, and Anypoint Platform environments.
subtopics.summary: Externalizing configuration with property files and Anypoint Platform environments lets the same Mule application run correctly in Dev, QA, and Production without code changes.
subtopics.content_html:
A well-built Mule application never hard-codes connection strings, credentials, or endpoint URLs inside its flows. Instead, it reads them from externalized configuration so the exact same packaged artifact can run in Development, QA, and Production simply by pointing it at a different set of properties. This is achieved through property placeholders and Anypoint Platform's Business Groups and Environments model.

Configuration Properties in Mule 4

Mule 4 uses the <configuration-properties> global element (backed by the Configuration Properties module) to load values from a YAML or .properties file at deployment time.

<configuration-properties file="config-${mule.env}.yaml" />

<http:listener-config name="HTTP_Listener_config">
  <http:listener-connection host="0.0.0.0" port="${https.port}" />
</http:listener-config>

<db:config name="Database_Config">
  <db:generic-connection
    url="${db.url}"
    user="${db.user}"
    password="${secure::db.password}" />
</db:config>

A matching YAML file might look like this:

https:
  port: "8081"
db:
  url: "jdbc:sqlserver://prod-db.internal:1433;databaseName=orders"
  user: "svc_orders_api"
api:
  timeoutMs: 5000

Selecting the Right File per Environment

A common pattern is to name property files per environment (config-dev.yaml, config-qa.yaml, config-prod.yaml) and pass the active environment name as a Java system property or CloudHub environment variable at deploy time, e.g. -M-Dmule.env=prod, so the correct file loads without changing the packaged artifact.

Secure Properties

Secrets such as passwords, client secrets, and API keys should never sit in plain text, even in a private Git repository. MuleSoft's Secure Properties approach (via the Secure Configuration Properties module) encrypts sensitive values with a key, and the encrypted values are referenced with the secure:: prefix, as shown in the db:password attribute above. The decryption key itself is passed at deploy time as an environment variable, never checked into source control.

<secure-properties:config name="Secure_Properties" file="config-prod.yaml" key="${secure.key}">
  <secure-properties:encrypt algorithm="AES" mode="CBC" />
</secure-properties:config>

Anypoint Platform Environments

Separately from property files, Anypoint Platform provides logical Environments (e.g., Design, Sandbox, Production) within a Business Group. Environments provide isolation for:

  • Deployed applications (an app deployed to the Sandbox environment is invisible from Production in Runtime Manager).
  • API Manager instances and policies (a policy applied in Sandbox does not affect the Production API instance).
  • Client applications and credentials registered in each environment.

Most organizations map environments roughly to their SDLC stages, though the names are configurable and there is no forced 1:1 mapping between an Anypoint environment and an application's own property-file environment naming.

CloudHub Environment Variables

Beyond property files, CloudHub lets you set environment-specific values directly as deployment properties in Runtime Manager (or via the Maven plugin's <properties> block), which are exposed to the running application the same way as command-line -M-D system properties. This is often used for values that change per deployment without needing a new build, such as feature flags or worker-specific tuning.

Key Points

  • Externalize all environment-specific values using property placeholders and the Configuration Properties module.
  • Keep separate YAML/properties files per environment and select the active one at deploy time.
  • Encrypt secrets with Secure Properties and inject the decryption key as an environment variable, never in source control.
  • Anypoint Platform Environments provide logical isolation for deployments, API Manager instances, and credentials, separate from your own property-file naming.
